newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: PESSIMISM REIGNS SUPREME ON SLOVAK EQUITIES MARKET.
newsitem.headline: PESSIMISM REIGNS SUPREME ON SLOVAK EQUITIES MARKET.

text.p: Slovakia's new securities law coupled with recent central bank monetary measures have dealt a severe blow to the country's capital market from which it will take months to recover, analysts said on Tuesday.
"If nothing changes for the better, our capital market will need at least half a year to recover from this blow," Vladimir Kuklis, an analyst of the CSOB bank, told Reuters.
Slovak shares began to fall near the end of August following the murky privatisation of blue chip oil and gas storage company Nafta.

Parliament's approval in October of a new securities law and new central bank new rules for foreign exchange positions for monetary purposes then added to the market's woes, as did signs of a slowing economy, analysts said.

"The privatisation of Nafta, which deeply shook foreign investors. The slow-down in the GDP growth and the precarious trade balance, would in themselves be enough to pull the market down," said Martin Barto of ING Barings.
"But add to that the non-standard amendment to the securities law which spread so much uncertainty, and I see a really gloomy future for the market at least in the short-term," he said.
The controversial securities law allows the majority stockholder of a company to arbitrarily suspend trading in the company's shares on the stock market.
Kuklis said that current credit interest rates of around 15 percent were also one of the main obstacles to larger investment injections to a market starved for cash.
And the prospect of a further rise due to central bank measures aimed at curbing loan expansion -- due to take effect from the beginning of next year -- has made the outlook even more pessimistic.
"It is hard to predict when rates may ease, but I am afraid that the entire package bodes drastically ill for further development of the whole economy," Kuklis said.

Legislative barriers have also held up some investors, analysts said, since Slovak law requires investors to hold shares for at least one year for them to be recognised as a portfolio investment and therefore qualify for relief from paying value-added-tax on these holdings.
